subsection: 1. The Family Law (Maintenance of Spouses and Children) Act 1976

notes.h: What the Act does and who is protected
notes.b: When a relationship breaks down, one person can be left without money to live on. The Family Law (Maintenance of Spouses and Children) Act 1976 gives a financially dependent spouse and dependent children a legal right to maintenance, which is regular financial support paid by one person for the benefit of a dependant (someone who relies on another for money).
points: A dependent spouse or civil partner is one who does not have the financial resources to support themselves, so the test for the right is dependency.
A dependent spouse can claim maintenance from the other spouse if the relationship breaks down and no other means of support is available. Spouses owe each other support according to their means.
Maintenance can be sought for the dependent spouse and for the dependent children, which is why the Act protects the whole family, not just one person.
Maintenance is regular support, not a one-off payment or a gift.
Maintenance covers the day-to-day costs of the dependant, such as food, clothing, housing and other necessities.
The amount depends on the means and needs of the people involved: the court considers what the paying person can afford and what the dependant needs.
notes.tip: Open an exam answer with a one-sentence meaning of maintenance. A dependent spouse is defined by lacking the resources to support themselves, not by who has custody of the children.

notes.h: Who counts as a dependent child, and who pays
notes.b: The Act sets exact limits on which children count as dependent, and these limits are the detail examiners reward. It also says who can be asked to pay and in what circumstances.
points: A dependent child is under 18, or aged 18 to under 23 and in full-time education, or a child of any age with a disability who cannot support themselves.
The payer for a spouse's maintenance is the other spouse, and for a child's maintenance it is either parent.
Maintenance can be sought whether the couple are living together or apart, so the payer can be ordered to pay even where the parents continue to share the same house after separating.
For a child, the marital status of the parents does not matter, so the parents of a child born outside marriage owe the child support too.
notes.tip: Students lose marks by leaving out the age limits for a dependent child, so give all three: under 18, under 23 in full-time education, and any age with a disability. Say that the right exists whether couples live together or apart.

notes.b: Getting maintenance follows three steps, moving from a private agreement to the courts only if the parties cannot agree.
points: 1. The parties try to reach a maintenance agreement, a written arrangement setting out the amount and how often payments are made. It is a private arrangement between them.
2. If no agreement can be reached, the dependant applies to court. The application goes to the District Court or the Circuit Court.
3. The court hears the application and, if it is granted, makes a maintenance order setting out how much the supporting spouse or parent must pay and how often.
A maintenance order is made by the court and can be enforced by it, whereas an informal agreement is not enforced in the same way, so an order gives the dependant stronger protection.
The court can vary (change) an order if circumstances change, for example if the payer's income falls or the child's needs grow.
notes.tip: A full answer on how the Act protects the family gives the route in order: agreement, then a District or Circuit Court order, then enforcement.

notes.b: A court order is only useful if the money actually arrives. When the payer stops paying, the court has a specific tool to collect it.
points: If the supporting spouse or parent fails to pay, the court can make an Attachment of Earnings Order.
An Attachment of Earnings Order deducts an amount from the wages of the person who owes maintenance and pays it directly to the dependant.
It matters because the dependant does not have to chase the payer, and the money arrives before the payer can spend it.
An Attachment of Earnings Order is not a fine or penalty. It is a way of collecting what is already owed.
Maintenance owed under a court order is enforceable, so the dependant can return to court if payments stop.
notes.tip: Name the order exactly, Attachment of Earnings Order, and say what it does: it deducts from wages and pays the dependant directly. The exact name earns a mark.

notes.h: Fitting the Act into the wider picture
notes.b: Family breakdown can involve separation or divorce, but the right to maintenance does not depend on which stage a couple has reached. The Act also has a limited job, which is money.
points: Separation: spouses live apart, either by private agreement or by court order; separation does not end the marriage.
Divorce: a legal process that ends a marriage, governed by the Family Law (Divorce) Act 1996 as amended by the Family Law Act 2019.
Maintenance can be claimed during a separation or after one, and can exist alongside a divorce, so the dependant's support is protected whatever the legal status of the marriage.
Protection under this Act is available whether the dependant is a spouse, a civil partner or a child, which is why it is described as protection for the whole family.
The Act deals with money (income). It does not deal with the home, violence or children at risk, because each of those has its own Act.
notes.tip: In a wider question on legal protection when a marriage breaks down, name the Act with one line: it provides maintenance for dependants. In a question on the rights and responsibilities of a couple, the duty to support a partner and children is credited under this Act.

keyTerms.definition: A spouse who does not have the financial resources to support themselves after a relationship breaks down.
Regular financial support paid by a spouse or parent to a dependant for everyday needs such as food, clothing and housing.
A private, written arrangement between the parties setting out the amount and frequency of maintenance payments.
A court order, made by the District Court, requiring a person to pay maintenance to a dependant.
A court order that deducts maintenance directly from the wages of the person who owes it.
The parent with whom a dependent child lives and who has day-to-day care of the child.
A person, such as a spouse or child, who relies on another for financial support and may claim maintenance under the Act.

factCards.term: Steps to obtain a maintenance order
factCards.definition: First try a maintenance agreement; if none is reached, apply to the District Court for a maintenance order.
An Attachment of Earnings Order deducts maintenance from the paying person's wages and pays it directly to the dependant.

factCards.term: Who can claim maintenance under the Act
factCards.definition: A dependent spouse or civil partner, and a parent with custody of a dependent child.
The District Court, which makes maintenance orders when parties cannot agree.

factCards.term: Effect of sharing a home on maintenance
factCards.definition: Maintenance remains payable to the custodial parent even where both parents still live in the same house.

questions.prompt: Explain how a dependent spouse can obtain maintenance under the Family Law (Maintenance of Spouses and Children) Act 1976.
questions.model: Maintenance is financial support for a dependant. First the parties may agree a written maintenance agreement setting out the amount and frequency of payments. If no agreement can be reached, the dependent spouse applies to the District Court for a maintenance order, and the court orders the other spouse to pay a set amount. If that spouse then fails to pay, the court can grant an Attachment of Earnings Order, which deducts the money from wages and pays it directly to the dependant.

questions.prompt: Outline the protection the Family Law (Maintenance of Spouses and Children) Act 1976 gives to families when a relationship breaks down.
questions.model: The Act protects dependent spouses and civil partners who lack the financial resources to support themselves, so a spouse can claim maintenance from the other spouse after a breakdown. It protects dependent children: the parent with custody is entitled to maintenance for the child even where the parents still share a home. Protection is put into practice through a maintenance agreement, or if none is reached, a maintenance order from the District Court. Enforcement is supported by Attachment of Earnings Orders, which take money directly from wages. Together these ensure that the dependant's everyday needs such as food, clothing and housing are met, whatever the legal status of the marriage.
